subject: Sampling from subset of elements in a matrix

messages.author: b70e5a419fc15914
messages.subject: Sampling from subset of elements in a matrix
parts:
Is it possible to use logical statements to assign priors to a subset of elements in a matrix?

In another thread, Josh suggested this solution, in order to fix location parameters in an IRT model:

ordered[K-1] bj_raw[J-1]; 
real<upper=0> bj_init_a;
real<lower=0> bj_init_b;

Then in the transformed parameters, declare vector[K-1] bj[J], and:

bj[1,1]<-bj_init_a; bj[1,2]<-0; bj[1,3]<-bj_init_b;
for (j in 2:J) {
bj[j]<-bj_raw[j-1];
}

If works well for a small matrix.  The priors can be assigned by:

bj_init_1 ~ normal(0,1);
 bj_init_3 ~ normal(0,1);
 for (j in 1:(J-1)) {
 bj_raw[j] ~ normal(0,1);
 }

What about a larger matrix, in which the fixed parameters are distributed more randomly?  Declaring, transforming, and sampling from a larger matrix might be prohibitively complicated.  Can it be done with logical statements?  I have a matrix of parameters (para_raw), a matrix of transformed parameters (para_trans), and an indexing matrix (index), with 1s at positions to sample and 0s at the positions to fix.  The elements of para_trans are either fixed or transformed from para_raw in the transformed parameters block.  The code in the model block goes something like:

for (r in 1:rows) {
for (c in 1:cols) {
if (index[r,c] != 0) 
para_raw[r,c] ~ normal(0,1); 
}
}

The model runs, but samples for all elements of para_raw, not only the 1s.  Is that because para_raw is declared as an r by c matrix?  Can STAN sample from only some elements of a declared variable, or does the variable need to be broken down into the elements to be estimated, as in Josh's code?  Is there some other way of accomplishing this?

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Sampling from subset of elements in a matrix
parts:
On Jul 19, 2014, at 5:13 PM, Katherine Grace Jonas <katherine....@gmail.com> wrote:

> Is it possible to use logical statements to assign priors to a subset of elements in a matrix?

Yes. But it can be problematic if the conditions in the logical
statements involve parameters, because it will usually introduce
a discontinuity and hence non-differentiability of the resulting
log posterior.

>
> In another thread, Josh suggested this solution, in order to fix location parameters in an IRT model:
>
> ordered[K-1] bj_raw[J-1];
> real<upper=0> bj_init_a;
> real<lower=0> bj_init_b;
>
> Then in the transformed parameters, declare vector[K-1] bj[J], and:
>
> bj[1,1]<-bj_init_a; bj[1,2]<-0; bj[1,3]<-bj_init_b;
> for (j in 2:J) {
> bj[j]<-bj_raw[j-1];
> }
Yes, this is one way to technically identify the location of an IRT model.

>
> If works well for a small matrix. The priors can be assigned by:
>
> bj_init_1 ~ normal(0,1);
> bj_init_3 ~ normal(0,1);
> for (j in 1:(J-1)) {
> bj_raw[j] ~ normal(0,1);
> }
>
> What about a larger matrix, in which the fixed parameters are distributed more randomly? Declaring, transforming, and sampling from a larger matrix might be prohibitively complicated. Can it be done with logical statements?

Yes, it can be done with logical statements.

You can also go to a more database-like input to deal with ragged arrays.
Something like:

int idx[K];
real param[K];

Where param[k] is the parameter with index idx[k].

> I have a matrix of parameters (para_raw), a matrix of transformed parameters (para_trans), and an indexing matrix (index), with 1s at positions to sample and 0s at the positions to fix. The elements of para_trans are either fixed or transformed from para_raw in the transformed parameters block. The code in the model block goes something like:
>
> for (r in 1:rows) {
> for (c in 1:cols) {
> if (index[r,c] != 0)
> para_raw[r,c] ~ normal(0,1);
> }
> }
>
> The model runs, but samples for all elements of para_raw, not only the 1s.

I'm not sure waht you mean by "the 1s". You mean index[r,c] == 1? You are
putting a prior only on the para_raw[r,c] parameters for which
index[r,c] != 0.

All of the values in a transformed parameter will be printed out, but
you will be able to see some that are fixed values (and thus have ill-defined
R-hat values) and no variance in the posterior.

> Is that because para_raw is declared as an r by c matrix? Can STAN sample from only some elements of a declared variable, or does the variable need to be broken down into the elements to be estimated, as in Josh's code? Is there some other way of accomplishing this?

Yes, see above.

- Bob
